newsitem.title: HONG KONG: France's Chirac to raise HK issues in China visit.
newsitem.headline: France's Chirac to raise HK issues in China visit.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac will raise concerns over possible threats to the rule of law and democracy in Hong Kong with Chinese leaders during a visit to Beijing in May, a leading Hong Kong democrat said on Tuesday.

Democratic Party leader Martin Lee, who is on a lobbying mission to France and Norway, said in a statement that the French government and leading parliamentarians had demonstrated strong support for democratic institutions in Hong Kong.

The British colony of more than 150 years reverts to Chinese rule on July 1 and has been promised a high degree of autonomy for the next 50 years under joint Sino-British treaties on Hong Kong's handover.
But with the handover just 140 days away, fears are mounting in the territory of 6.3 million people that its freedoms and democratic institutions will be crippled.
Hailing his visit so far as being "extremely successful", Lee said he held meetings in Paris with French Justice Minister Jacques Toubon and Senate head Rene Monory, among others.
"Mr Toubon showed a clear understanding of the threats to the rule of law in Hong Kong," Lee said in a statement.

"He reiterated the French government's support for the full implementation of the Joint Declaration and for elected institutions and stated the French President, Jacques Chirac, would raise these issues on his trip to Beijing and Hong Kong in May," the statement said.
Chirac is expected to pay a state visit to China in mid-May.
Foreign ministry sources contacted in Paris said France has been clearly backing full implementation of the joint declaration.
But no confirmation was immediately available on Chirac's intentions or the outcome of Lee's discussions with Toubon.
Lee, a vocal critic of some of China's policies on Hong Kong, has made several trips to Western countries in the past year to try to lobby for support.

Lee and other pro-democracy Hong Kong activists are particularly opposed to a recently formed China-backed provisional lawmaking chamber which will replace Hong Kong's elected legislative council upon the handover.

Lee will be in the Norwegian capital Oslo over the next few days where he is expected to meet Norwegian Minister for Foreign Affairs Bjoern Tore Godal, State Secretary Jan Egeland and other officials.
